newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. B727 upgrade costs to hit air freight sector.
newsitem.headline: U.S. B727 upgrade costs to hit air freight sector.

text.p: The air freight industry is bracing for a U.S. government order that could drastically reduce the amount of freight carried on many Boeing 727 freighters until costly safety upgrades are made.

The airworthiness directive from the Federal Aviation Administration(FAA) is likely to affect 321 B-727s worldwide - those converted from passenger aircraft by certain after-market refurbishers rather than Boeing.

The FAA is concerned that under certain adverse flying conditions, floors bearing the maximum allowable payload weight assigned each pallet position could buckle. The FAA wants floors, sidewalls and cargo doors reinforced.
The directive would apply to U.S. registered 727s, but authorities elsewhere likely would require the modifications as well.

Excluding revenue losses because of payload reductions, the cost of the modifications has been estimated by one contractor at $425,000 per aircraft, and $400,000 to $500,000 by another, the aviation finance journal Commercial Aviation Report(CAR) said.
The largest operator of affected aircraft is Federal Express Corp, with 122. In Europe, the largest operator is DHL Worldwide Express, with 12. DHL also has 13 in its U.S. network.
Other major operators are Express One with 21 aircraft, Emery Worldwide with 17, and American International Airways and Kitty Hawk Air Cargo, with 15 each.
Industry sources now expect the FAA to issue the draft directive by the end of April or early May. Interested parties would have several weeks in which to comment before the order takes effect.
Until the upgrades are completed, the FAA has proposed curbs on maximum cargo allowances by up to 73 percent per pallet position.

This has brought a hail of objections from operators, who say that is too severe. The 727 is rated at a maximum 10,000 pounds per pallet position, but may be allowed to carry no more than 2,700-3,000 pending the upgrades, said industry sources.
While few carriers actually carry 10,000 pounds per position, such a reduction would be significant, CAR said adding that operators have pressed the FAA for a 6,000-pound cap.
For FedEx alone, analysts' estimates of the revenue impact range up to $1 million a day at the outset of the retrofit programme, CAR editor Scott Hamilton told Reuters.
But this also assumes that payload reductions are closer to what the FAA originally proposed.
Major operators are saying little.
"We're working with the FAA and don't have anything (on) preparations in anticipation of what might or might not happen," FedEx spokeswoman Diane Faquin told Reuters.
The FAA directive is likely to call for a package of fixes, which could be done at once or spread out to minimize aircraft down time.

In an interview with CAR, Thomas McSweeney, FAA director of aircraft certification is quoted as saying the federal agency did not order an immediate grounding of the 727s because of the need to research both the problem and the proposed fix thoroughly before ordering such a drastic remedy.
While the problem is real, the statistical chances of an accident occuring in the very near term are "infinitesimal", said McSweeny.
"So we have got to weigh all the consequences of our actions according to what it is we are proposing to do because the laws require us" to consider economic and social impacts as well, he said.
The FAA is acting now because of computer modelling which was not available at the time of the original conversions, said Hamilton.

Earlier this year, similar concerns caused the FAA to call for structural upgrades to eight converted Boeing 747-100 freighters, and McSweeny suggested that the FAA may look next at the adequacy of freight conversions for DC-8s and Boeing 737s. -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
